newsitem.title: UK: Rates and strong sterling set to hurt UK trade.
newsitem.headline: Rates and strong sterling set to hurt UK trade.

text.p: British exporters will soon start to feel the pinch as sterling's recent strength looks set to continue after a quarter-point rise in UK base rates to 6.0 percent, analysts said on Thursday.
Further gains for the pound coupled with slow growth among Britain's main trading partners in Europe could nudge British exporters out of the market.
"The odds are against them at the moment. I'd be surprised if exporters can escape unscathed," said Jonathan Loynes, UK economist at HSBC Markets.
"Exports have held up remarkably robustly so far this year but you've got to ask yourself whether that can continue," he said.

The Confederation of British Industry's (CBI) survey of industrial trends for October, published last week, showed no damage to export optimism and a pick-up in export order books to the highest level since April 1995.

Loynes said when the survey was taken sterling was trading at around 2.38 marks but since then there has been significant further appreciation. At 1130 GMT on Thursday, sterling was trading at around 2.46 marks.
"Obviously there has got to be a worry that if the pound goes much further exporters are really going to struggle," said Loynes.

Douglas Godden, head of the economic policy group at the CBI, said the concern among manufacturers would be dependent on how much further sterling increased and whether the acceleration was sustained.
"The interest rate increase will underpin sterling. If it were to go up to around 2.50 marks and stay there for a while it would be a concern and would affect exporters' profit margins," he said.

British exporters, particularly in the manufacturing sector, have lagged the economic recovery, hampered by weak growth among Britain's main trading partners as European countries strive to meet the Maastricht criteria to qualify for European Economic and Monetary Union.

The lack of overseas demand left manufacturers with mountains of unsold stocks on their shelves, produced when times were better. Those stocks have had to be sold before manufacturing output perks up again, although there are signs that has now happened.
There are also suggestions that manufacturers were trying to make themselves more competitive with data in recent months showing exports were holding up and export prices falling.

Some analysts were sceptical about the plight of manufacturers. The complaints that a stronger currency was limiting their potential would not be completely justified, they said, because key European markets are on the road to recovery.

"They will still do pretty well relative to where they are now because if Germany and France are accelerating, the growth in the overseas market share will easily offset the modest errosion of competitiveness which we are seeing at the moment," said Kevin Gardiner, UK economist at Morgan Stanley.
"You have to remember we are starting from a position at which the pound was spectacularly cheap to begin with," he said.
He also said strong consumer spending on Britain's high streets will inevitably feed through to the manufacturing base.
"I would be amazed if we can have a consumer boom and a fixed investment surge with domestic manufacturing losing out," said Gardiner. "Of course they won't, they'll benefit."
But, he said the balance of trade would deteriorate as the level of imports rose. "It will widen alongside solid growth in exports and very rapid growth in manufacturing production."
